prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction and experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall effect and time-reversal-invariant topological insulators

statement.case_for: B030 combines a sharp, original theoretical idea (the Z2 classification and the Kane-Mele quantum spin Hall proposal) with a decisive experimental observation (edge transport in HgTe/CdTe quantum wells by Molenkamp's group). It has been confirmed by many independent groups and materials for more than fifteen years, the interpretation is stable, and it opened topological band theory across condensed matter, photonics and materials science. It is a prediction-then-discovery prize of the classic kind, and it is the only candidate on which two members, Danielsson and I, placed first, with four top-three rankings in all. Support for B030 is broad rather than concentrated: members from different subfields rank it in their top four.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the real weakness. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, which pointed experimentalists to HgTe, is not among the credited names, and Hasan's 3D topological insulator work is a separate, equally weighty experimental line. Any three-person set omits a legitimate contributor, and a citation naming 'quantum spin Hall' alone would sit awkwardly with the 3D materials. The 2016 prize on topological phases also invites the argument that this area has already been honoured, although that prize concerned topological phase transitions and the integer quantum Hall effect, not time-reversal-invariant systems.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B030 fourth and would credit Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, reflecting that BHZ, Molenkamp and Hasan all matter and that Mele's role is the most substitutable.
responses.response: I take the point that the experimental credit is wider than Molenkamp alone, and I cannot fully rebut it. But the prediction of the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall effect in graphene is the originating idea, and it was Kane and Mele together who made it. Dropping Mele, who co-authored both seminal 2005 papers, to make room for Hasan would split the theory credit awkwardly and make the citation less coherent. I prefer Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, with the citation worded around the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators so that the 3D work is not excluded by the text, even though it is not credited by name.

responses.point: Eriksson places B021 first because the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and the Jarillo-Herrero discovery form a clean theory-plus-experiment pair with very rapid and broad follow-on work across moire materials.
responses.response: I agree the attribution in B021 is cleaner than in B030, and the speed of follow-on work is remarkable. My reservation is maturity: the field is about eight years old, the mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, and parallel experimental work by Dean, Young, Yazdani and others is not credited. A topological insulator prize rests on results that have been stable for fifteen years. I would not oppose B021 later, but I do not think its case is stronger today, and I would like the committee to weigh how much interpretive uncertainty it is willing to accept.

responses.point: Danielsson also ranks B030 first as a clean prediction-and-confirmation case that is arguably overdue, and ranks B033 (ATLAS and CMS Higgs discovery) second as an experimental achievement not yet honoured.
responses.response: I agree with him on B030 and on the overdue timing. On B033 I share the view that the experimental discovery of the Higgs boson deserves recognition, and my experience in detector-building collaborations makes me sympathetic to the scientific case. But I ranked it eighth, because the credit problem is severe: thousands of people, two experiments, and three founding names who are a proxy rather than a clear attribution. I think it fails on attribution now, not on merit, and I would not put it into the preferred configuration unless the committee can agree on a defensible citation.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B002) first and trapped ions (B006) second, valuing the platform architecture that underlies nearly all superconducting quantum processors and the thirty-year record of trapped-ion quantum information.
responses.response: The importance of circuit QED is clear, but the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits is close enough that awarding the field again so soon would need a strong argument for why this is a distinct achievement. Trapped ions face a similar overlap with the 2012 prize for Wineland and Haroche. I am less convinced than Johansson that the quantum-computing platforms are ready for recognition ahead of a field with a clearer discovery narrative, and I would want to see the case that the architecture and gate contributions are separable from the earlier prizes.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks (B024) first as the clearest advance in measurement precision, with a clean two-person credit of Katori and Ye.
responses.response: I agree that the credit is clean and that the 10^-18 results are independently confirmed. I ranked it sixth, not higher, because Ye's work is partly entangled with the frequency-comb prize of 2005 and with the 2012 prize on single quantum systems, and the practical payoff, such as the redefinition of the second, is still ahead of us. It is a strong candidate for a later year, and I would put it ahead of B021 on attribution cleanliness but not on lasting conceptual influence.

uncertainties: Whether a three-name set including Mele, as opposed to Hasan or a BHZ author, best reflects the decisive contributions.
Whether the citation should name the quantum spin Hall effect alone or the broader class of time-reversal-invariant topological insulators, given that the 3D work is not credited.
How much weight the 2016 topological-phases prize should carry against a second topological award.
I rely on my recollection of priority chronology rather than independently verified sources.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My documented connections (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur, KTH astroparticle group) do not involve any credited candidate on the shortlist. My own field of experimental astroparticle physics is outside most shortlisted topics, so I rely on the supplied evidence and colleagues for condensed-matter and quantum-optics judgments.
